That's just knowledge you should know" B, T and NK cells: "when you hear the word humoral, think B-cell response"; the plasma cell ("associate that with antibody production and release"); helper (CD4) and cytotoxic (CD8) T cells, which read antigen on MHC; and NK cells, with no B or T markers, CD16 and ADCC, and his schematic of how MHC class I holds them back Innate versus adaptive immunity, and what belongs to each Primary versus secondary lymphoid organs: "the thymus and the bone marrow for our class" (GALT is not primary), "bone marrow, B cells, thymus, T cells," and the stroma: "epithelioreticular cells, you should associate that with the thymus" The thymus (cortex and medulla, involution to fat, 95 to 99 percent of thymocytes selected out, the blood-thymus barrier, thymic education) and the lymph node (the sinuses the lymph runs through, and where B and T cells are activated, multiply and make antibody) The spleen: "the main thing is just to really associate this PALS with the spleen," the T cell sheath around the central artery; the white and red pulp, the marginal zone and the splenic sinuses What he said won't be asked: stained images ("I'm not gonna ask you any questions specifically on stained images") and the typical concentration of each cell 1 Recognizing the blood cells and their jobs: red cells (most of the cells) carry oxygen and carbon dioxide, platelets come from megakaryocytes ("just knowledge you should know") and start clotting, and the white cells come in two classes and five types: the granulocytes and the agranulocytes (monocytes and lymphocytes), each with its share, most to least common, its nucleus and its line in the hematopoiesis tree Study guide + recording · 6 questions in the bank Know this Dr. Herr's guide to his own lecture, and it asks for general roles and basic organization. Recognize each blood cell and know its job: red cells carry oxygen and carbon dioxide, platelets (megakaryocyte fragments) start clotting, neutrophils kill bacteria, eosinophils fight parasites and allergy, basophils hold heparin, monocytes become macrophages. Then B cells (antibodies), T cells (CD4 helpers, CD8 killers) and NK cells; the bone marrow and thymus as primary organs versus the nodes, MALT and spleen as secondary; and the layout of the thymus (cortex, medulla), lymph node (B-cell follicles, T-cell paracortex) and spleen (white pulp with its PALS of T cells around the central arteriole, red pulp). Platelets are pieces of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow, and they take part in clotting. Hematology is the study of the blood and its cells. Blood holds three kinds of cells. The erythrocytes, the red blood cells, are most of them, about 99 percent of the cells in the blood, and they carry oxygen and carbon dioxide; oxygen transport is their main job. The platelets are pieces of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow, and they initiate blood clotting: he said they play a role in the clotting cascade. "Remember, platelets arise from megakaryocytes. That's just knowledge you should know." The rest are the white blood cells, or leukocytes, and "what you need to remember with white blood cells is we've got two classes and 5 types." 2 The white cells' jobs: the neutrophil (multi-lobed, about 10 hours in the blood, the first line of defense against bacteria), eosinophil (red granules, major basic protein against parasites, allergy), basophil (dark blue granules, heparin, asthma) and monocyte (becomes the macrophage and expresses MHC II) Study guide + recording · 8 questions in the bank Their granules hold two weapons. Peroxidase binds to microorganisms and helps kill them. Major basic protein, MBP, also called PRG2, binds to and disrupts the membranes of parasites, both protozoa and helminths (worms), and it also makes basophils release histamine. Eosinophils and basophils both have a bilobed nucleus and IgE receptors. Tell them apart by the granules: red with eosin (the eosinophil: peroxidase and major basic protein, parasites and allergy) or dark blue to purple (the basophil: heparin and histamine, asthma). 3 B and T cells: B cells carry surface IgM and IgD, and a B cell whose antibody fits an antigen recruits helper T cells and becomes a plasma cell that releases that antibody, in a secondary organ; helper T cells (CD4, antigen on MHC II) help the B cells, cytotoxic T cells (CD8) kill what they bind, and T cells carry memory Study guide + recording · 5 questions in the bank Know this A B cell whose antibody fits its antigen recruits helper T cells and becomes a plasma cell, which releases that antibody; in a lymph node, plasma cells secrete it in the medulla. B lymphocytes carry the humoral response: "if you hear the word humoral, you're thinking B lymphocyte, you're thinking antibody production in some form or fashion." Each B cell makes and displays membrane-bound antibodies, IgM and IgD, which act as its receptors for antigens, and each mature B cell answers one antigen. His drawing showed it: a B cell whose antibody doesn't fit a star-shaped antigen can't bind it, but one whose antibody fits does. That binding generates a chemical signal that recruits helper T cells, and the B cell transforms into a plasma cell, which makes a great many antibodies like the one that bound and releases them into the circulation. 4 NK cells: the large lymphocytes, with no B or T markers and no specific receptors; MHC class I on a healthy cell binds the inhibitory receptor and stops the killing, a cell missing it is killed, and too many activating ligands cause induced killing; CD16 binds IgG's constant region in ADCC, with macrophages, neutrophils and eosinophils Study guide + recording · 6 questions in the bank Know this MHC class I on a healthy cell binds the NK cell's inhibitory receptor and stops the killing; a cell missing it is killed; far more activating ligands cause induced killing. In ADCC, circulating antibodies bind the antigens on a target cell's surface. The Fc receptors on NK cells, macrophages, neutrophils and eosinophils then bind the antibody-coated target, and the killer cell secretes lytic enzymes, perforins, TNF and granzymes (his slide's list), which together kill the target. The antibody picks the target and the killer cell does the killing, with no T cell receptor and no MHC involved. His ADCC picture puts a target cell in the middle with an NK cell, a neutrophil, an eosinophil and a macrophage around it: he had presented them one by one, but "they all play a role in concert together." A healthy cell shows both the activating ligand and MHC class I. The activating receptor wants to bind the ligand, but the inhibitory receptor binds the MHC class I and stops that response: no killing. A target cell, such as a tumor cell or a virus-infected cell, still has the activating ligand but is missing its MHC class I, the signal that says "cut it out." The activating receptor binds the ligand, and the NK cell kills the target. 5 Innate versus adaptive immunity: what the body just does (barriers, low pH, lysozyme, thiocyanate, interferons, phagocytes, NK cells), versus the antibodies of the humoral arm ("think B-cell response") and the T cells of the cellular arm Study guide + recording · 4 questions in the bank Know this Humoral means B cells and antibodies; cellular means T cells, which target transformed cells. Nonspecific, or innate, immunity is what "your body just does": pre-existing defenses against microbial invasion, in place without any sequence of events to set them off. It has five parts: physical barriers, the skin and mucous membranes; chemical defenses, such as the low pH of some regions of the body; secretory substances, such as lysozyme, thiocyanate (in saliva) and interferons; phagocytic cells, the macrophages, neutrophils and monocytes; and the natural killer (NK) cells. Specific, or adaptive, immunity produces acquired resistance, and it takes a sequence of events. A first contact with a specific antigen starts a chain of reactions carried out by the effector B and T cells, and it often leaves a state of immune memory. It has two arms, which aren't independent: they act together. The humoral response belongs to the B cells: they make antibodies, which mark invaders for destruction by other cells. The cellular immune response belongs to the T cells: it targets transformed cells and virus-infected cells for destruction. His shortcut: "When you hear the word humoral, think B-cell response. And then also, when you hear B cells, think about the production of antibodies." 6 Primary versus secondary lymphoid organs: the primary ones are just the bone marrow and the thymus (not GALT), where B and T cells become immunocompetent without antigen ("bone marrow, B cells, thymus, T cells"; self-reactive B cells removed in the marrow); every other one, lymph nodes, MALT and GALT, and the spleen, is secondary Study guide + recording · 5 questions in the bank He narrowed the long list: "Really, what we want to remember is lymph nodes, MALT and GALT, and spleen. We'll look at the tonsils as well." The activation of B and T cells takes place in these peripheral, or secondary, organs: the cells originate in the primary organs, the self-reactive ones are removed, and the rest are sent out to be further educated and made into what they need to be. The secondary organs capture antigens and give lymphocytes a place to undergo clonal proliferation and differentiate into effector cells in the presence of those antigens. Each has its own job: the lymph nodes filter lymph; MALT and GALT, sitting with the epithelia, are the first defense against external antigens; and the spleen filters blood. 7 The spleen: the PALS, the T cell sheath around the central artery ("associate this PALS with the spleen"); the splenic artery from the celiac trunk bringing blood-borne antigens in, with no afferent lymphatics; white pulp and red pulp; the marginal zone; red pulp of cords and sinusoids; and what the spleen does Study guide + recording · 8 questions in the bank Know this The PALS, the T cell sheath around the central artery of the white pulp, means the spleen: "if you see a central artery, that's where you have that area of PALS." The spleen, a secondary lymphoid organ, filters blood and responds to systemic, blood-borne infections. It lies in the upper left quadrant of the abdomen, behind the stomach and just below the diaphragm. In adults it is the largest lymphoid organ, about the size of a clenched fist. At its hilum, the large splenic artery, a branch of the celiac trunk, enters with the nerves, and it carries the blood-borne antigens and lymphocytes into the spleen. The splenic vein and lymphatics leave there. It has no afferent lymphatics; its efferent lymphatics leave at the hilum. The white pulp is islands of lymphoid tissue around a central arteriole (he called it the central artery), which comes from the splenic artery after many treelike branchings. In it he pointed out a primary follicle, a marginal zone, germinal centers and the PALS, the periarteriolar lymphatic sheath: the lymphocytes wrapped around the arteriole ("peri means around"), which "I'll just say is associated with the T-cell area." "The main thing is just to really associate this PALS with the spleen," he said, and at the end: "If you see a central artery, that's where you have that area of PALS." Lymphoid nodules lie farther out in the white pulp, and they are the B cells: primary nodules, or secondary ones with germinal centers, as in the lymph nodes. A nodule pushes the arteriole off to one side. Around the white pulp is a shell of sparsely cellular lymphoid tissue, the marginal zone, with macrophages and some B cells (his slide). 8 The thymus: epithelioreticular cells form its stroma ("I do want you to know that"), reticular cells and type III collagen everywhere else; the dense, dark cortex versus the lighter medulla; the blood-thymus barrier's three layers; and involution to fat by the teens Study guide + recording · 6 questions in the bank Know this Every lymphoid organ's stroma is reticular cells and type III collagen except the thymus's, which is epithelioreticular cells. Every lymphoid organ's cells sit in a stroma, an internal framework of cells, and the blood that flows into the organ passes through it, where it meets many cells and can set off many reactions. In every lymphoid organ except the thymus, the stroma is reticular cells and reticulin fibers, which are type III collagen. The thymus is the exception: its stroma is the cell processes of the epithelioreticular cells. "I do want you to know that. So epithelioreticular cells, you should associate that with the thymus." It is very large when you are born and little: largest and most active in the newborn and before adolescence, about 12 to 15 grams at birth and 30 to 40 grams by puberty (his slide's numbers). By the time you are a teenager, or a little past then, it shrinks, which is thymic involution, and fat replaces it. He said that in a donor you see a lot of fat in front of the heart: that is where the old thymus was. 9 The lymph node: the lymph's route (afferent lymphatic, subcapsular sinus, trabecular sinuses, efferent lymphatic); activation in the paracortex and follicles, B cells multiplying in germinal centers and plasma cells secreting antibody in the medulla; B cells in the follicles and T cells in the paracortex; dendritic and follicular dendritic cells; blood lymphocytes entering through high endothelial venules Study guide + recording · 8 questions in the bank His schematic follows the lymph. An afferent lymphatic vessel, with valves that direct the flow, brings lymph from the surrounding tissues into the subcapsular sinus, just under the capsule. From there it runs into the trabecular sinuses, beside the trabeculae, with the chance to pass through a germinal center on the way, and it leaves in the efferent lymphatic vessel. Around the sinuses are the outer cortex, with its superficial and deep layers, and the inner medulla, and blood comes into the node too, through its own capillaries. His slide adds how the filtering works: the sinus walls let the lymph percolate into the superficial and deep cortex, where the lymphocytes carry out immunosurveillance, and macrophages reach into the sinuses and phagocytose antigens and foreign material. Lymphocytes also arrive from the blood. Blood comes in through an artery at the hilum, and its lymphocytes cross into the deep cortex through the high endothelial venules, HEVs. T cells and dendritic cells are directed to the paracortex, and B cells to the cortex. Both leave the node through the efferent lymphatic vessel. The lymph node is the only lymphoid structure with both afferent and efferent lymphatics. 10 T cell education: precursors in through postcapillary venules, out to the cortex, positive and negative selection, single CD4 or CD8 cells out to the secondary organs, and 95 to 99 percent selected out by apoptosis Study guide + recording · 2 questions in the bank Then come positive and negative selection, which most of the cells fail; his slide puts them in order. In the cortex, the epithelioreticular cells present antigen on MHC molecules: a thymocyte whose receptor recognizes them survives, and one that doesn't dies. This is positive selection. The survivors move into the medulla for negative selection, which eliminates the cells aimed at self antigen displayed on self MHC. The cells that pass both become CD8-positive cytotoxic or CD4-positive helper T cells, ready for an immune response, and they leave through postcapillary venules into the circulation and migrate to the secondary lymphoid organs. 11 The splenic sinuses and the blood's path: rod-shaped, loosely packed endothelial cells with macrophage processes, strands of basal lamina at right angles, no smooth muscle and no pericytes; in the open circulation, sheathed capillaries empty into the cords Study guide + recording · 3 questions in the bank The splenic sinuses are special sinusoidal vessels. They are lined by rod-shaped, loosely packed endothelial cells that run lengthwise, with slit-like spaces between them, and macrophage processes reach between the cells to monitor the passing blood for foreign antigens. They have only strands of basal lamina, which loop around the endothelial cells at right angles, like the hoops around the staves of a leaky barrel. They have no smooth muscle and no pericytes. Blood cells move across the wall by squeezing through the slits (his slide). 12 MALT and the tonsils: Peyer's patches in the ileum, under M cells that take microbes from the lumen; the pharyngeal, tubal (at the auditory tube), palatine and lingual tonsils, and the crypts that trap material; IgA into the lumen, and adenoiditis Recording + objectives · 8 questions in the bank the tubal tonsils, at the torus tubarius, where the auditory tube opens; Together they form Waldeyer's ring, a broken circle of lymphoid tissue around the entrance to the nasopharynx and oropharynx. They sit where you breathe, eat and drink all day, so they start the response early: if you just ate a salmonella chicken sandwich, he said, it doesn't stop you from getting sick, but it starts to mount the response. The palatine tonsils have tonsillar crypts, where substances get wedged in, which gives the tissue a longer time to respond. Also flagged in class Granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) have prominent granules; agranulocytes (monocytes and lymphocytes) don't. The primary lymphoid organs are just the bone marrow and the thymus; any other lymphoid organ, GALT included, is secondary. B and NK cells form and mature in the marrow; T cell precursors leave it immunoincompetent and mature in the thymus. In the thymus, 95 to 99 percent of thymocytes fail selection and die by apoptosis; macrophages clear them.
